I have been doing people analytics for nine years and here is what I learned. Nobody reads your report. I send about forty pages every quarter and I know, from the system, that most people open it for less than two minutes. So now I do it differently. Every report starts with three numbers and one sentence about what they mean. Not thirty numbers. Three. For example, last quarter: seventy-eight per cent answered, six extra hours a week in the north, and nine hundred open comments. And then the sentence: people are not tired of the company, they are tired of the hours. That sentence took me two days to write and it is the only part anybody remembers. The other thirty-nine pages are for the people who ask, and honestly, not many people ask.

I read about two hundred CVs a week, and most of them say the same thing. Responsible for recruitment. Responsible for training. Responsible for culture. I have no idea if that means five people or five thousand. Now look at the difference one number makes. Instead of responsible for recruitment, write: hired thirty-eight people last year for a company of six hundred. Instead of responsible for engagement, write: ran the survey for six hundred people, seventy-eight per cent answered. Same job, same person, completely different reading. And you do not need many numbers. Two or three are enough for a whole CV. One more thing, and it matters for people who are not native speakers. Numbers are easy English. You do not need a big vocabulary to say thirty-eight people in six hundred. So use the part of English you already have.

Four hundred and seventy people answered, out of six hundred and twelve. That is a response rate of seventy-eight per cent. It is twelve points more than last year. So people are talking to us again, and most of the comments are about time.
